India Inc bullish on growth story: KM Birla
articles.text: India Inc.'s conviction in the country's growth prospects is possibly the highest in a long time and capital discipline is being mistaken for lack of commitment toward expanding capacities, said Kumar Mangalam Birla, chairman, Aditya Birla Group, at The Economic Times World Leaders Forum.There is enough capacity buildout happening on the ground with new plants springing up across the country and bank loan numbers pointing to robust economic activity, said the chief of the cement to consumer conglomerate valued at more than $118 billion. "I don't think we should confuse capital discipline with conviction about India,'' Birla said in a fireside chat with ET's Sruthijith KK. "Advances to corporates from banks have gone up by 20% compared to last year... and that is pretty evenly spread between small and medium enterprises as well." While the macro economy has been growing at the fastest pace among major peers, Indian industry is being blamed for not being aggressive in expanding capacities as new plants are coming up slower than in the past. Companies which binged on debt in the past cycles have been deleveraging and are a lot more cautious in expanding capacities to avoid repeating past mistakes. Birla, whose group itself has lined up $30 billion to expand capacities, said investment decisions are taken considering several factors including returns, volatility, industry needs and global events. "It is more of a capital discipline exercise,'' he said.ALSO READ | India Inc’s got all it takes to roll out ‘World+1’ model, says KM BirlaIn the last few years, the Aditya Birla Group has grown across most of its businesses amid a pandemic, wars, interest rate hikes, tariffs and energy shocks. The global economy seems to have grown "shock absorbers" in this period, and individual economies as well as corporations are learning to deal with a lot more stress, Birla said. "There are no more perma-friends or perma-enemies. There are only perma-issues," he said. The diversified conglomerate has taken a contrarian view in this period to grow across its traditional as well as new growth platforms. "It's been a two-part strategy," Birla said. For its overseas businesses, the group wants to be a "multi-local," setting up manufacturing plants close to consumers. "So, we have the supply chain flexibility and are not impacted by tariff wars or geopolitical bigotries," he said.ALSO READ | ET WLF 2026: Private players discuss India’s path from defence importer to global powerHindalco Industries' integrated aluminium plant being set up at Bay Minette in North America for a capital expenditure of $5 billion, for instance, is meant to primarily cater to customers in North America, Birla said.The growth in businesses in India, meanwhile, is reflecting the country's economy and its story, he said. "You need a strong economy to produce strong businesses. People talk about China+1 for India, and whilst that's a convenient shorthand, it's intellectually very lazy," Birla said. The narrative for India should now move to World+1, given that India has the capabilities and track record, and can be a "growth engine" for the world, he said.Lack of ease in doing business is not unique to India and almost every country and region has its own issues, he said, citing an example of how in an advanced economy one of his companies had to shift the plant's location due to environmental issues after working on it for months. "We are not the only people who have issues like land, environment, judicial, local laws etc," he said.The Aditya Birla Group is the largest producer of cement, refined copper, cellulosic fibre in the country besides housing the largest branded and lifestyle entity. It is also one of the largest producers of aluminium domestically, and a dominant player in paints, telecom and non-banking financial services. Several of its businesses are seeing high competitive intensity. "An important part of running a business is to compete and compete well. And risk-taking is an important part too, or you might as well not be in business," he said. While it is good to have a "rear view" of competition, the group focuses on doing what it does best-running plants and investing deeply in its ecosystems, he said. "We have very deep customer relationships. We have increased capacity exponentially. When you have been in industries for a long time, there is an accumulated knowledge that you have the advantage of," he said.Birla said the telecom business, which has been challenging for years, has turned the corner and it would be a credible and a profitable "number three" player as it invests in 4G and 5G.Novelis, its North American aluminium business, has stabilised after a fire accident and is ramping up. Plans to list are off the table as the company hasn't been getting the valuation that it hoped for. "We have no compulsion to do an IPO. There is no need for us to raise funds, so I don't see that happening now at all," he said.The world's largest producer of flat-rolled aluminium products, Novelis was to have listed in the US in 2024. "We put back the plans at that time because we were not getting the kind of value discovery that we thought or hoped we would or we were told we would. There was no other reason to want to list," Birla said.Hindalco's focus would now be to commission and ramp up the plant at Bay Minette, which will be pivotal for the company's future, he said.

articles.text:
China's "Manned Space" program issued a terse announcement on Sunday regarding its much-anticipated Chang’e 7 lunar exploration mission.

The agency stated: "In keeping with the principle of proceeding prudently and reliably, and ensuring absolute success, after a comprehensive assessment it has been determined that the Chang’e 7 mission does not meet the conditions for launch and therefore cannot be carried out during the planned launch window this year."

The Chinese message offered no explanation for the cause of the delay from the Wenchang Space Launch Site, located on an island in the South China Sea. Consisting of a lunar orbiter, lander, rover, and a mini-hopper of a probe, the mission was due to launch as early as Sunday on a Long March 5 rocket. It is intended to land at the South Pole of the Moon.

How Cursor beat Git's scalability shortcomings
articles.text: Developers recently burned by GitHub’s system outages should take note that there are other ways to manage Git at scale. One approach, recently put into action by Cursor, is to build the distributed version control system on object storage. A recent post from Cursor principal systems engineer Vicent Martí explains how the SpaceX subsidiary worked through its scaling issues with the notoriously fickle Git distributed version control system. The post explains how Cursor arrived at an architecture for its own Git-based repository service called Origin, which is powered by an internal engine called Continuity. A beta of the service is available with paid Cursor plans. “Agents have fundamentally changed the way we work with software, and in many ways they've made this situation worse. More code, more PRs, more CI runs. Version control is at the core of all of this, and it is possibly the hardest thing to change overnight,” Martí wrote. Martí speaks from experience, having worked at GitHub through much of the last decade when the company arrived at its own current architecture for managing Git. Synchronization is a bitch Git creator Linus Torvalds designed his software to work as a content-addressable data store, where all the objects are stored and indexed by the SHA-1 hash of their contents. Git sees a repository as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), with each commit being a node in a graph of nodes all connected by pointers. A Git server can look up an object directly by its SHA, but if it doesn’t have the SHA, then it “must actually walk the DAG step by step,” Martí noted. A client may just want to fetch or clone a consolidated packfile of the repository, or even get a list of recent changes, but to fulfill these requests, the server must traverse the entire graph only to assemble the necessary objects. Now, imagine providing such a service for over 400 million repositories, and you’ll get an idea of the scale at which GitHub operates (or struggles to do). After some fiddling about, GitHub engineers landed on what they called Spokes, which basically involves keeping at least three tightly synchronized copies of every repository on speedy NVMe disks. The approach became an industry standard, though over time its limits became apparent; the chief one is that the more replicas you make, the longer the synchronization takes. And Git does not play well with “eventual consistency,” Martí explained. Plus, these days agents bring their own mayhem. “When agents work with Git repositories at scale, they often operate outside of a monorepo by creating vast numbers of small repositories, many of them throwaway, and most of them barely touched,” Martí wrote. Object stores to the rescue When Cursor set out to build its own Git repository, it turned to object storage. Unlike file or block storage, object storage gives each chunk of bits its own unique identifier and files it with all the others in a single namespace (no directories). The most popular object storage today is Amazon Web Services’ Simple Storage Service (S3), which is increasingly used as a foundational layer for enterprise software such as databases, container registries and message brokers, thanks to its low cost, built-in redundancy and – for all practical purposes – endless scalability. With Origin, pushes are uploaded into S3 in a write-ahead log (WAL), capturing all changes as immutable objects. Wherever possible, changes are bundled together for faster throughput. Simultaneously, the pushes are written to the local “reference” copy of the repository (usually an NVMe disk). Once both actions complete, other replicas of the repository can download the changes as needed. “With the only requirement of having to synchronize the reference transaction with a single local repository instead of a quorum of replicas, we have a system that can ingest pushes as fast as our disk allows,” Martí wrote. Git will still have to do DAG traversal for many operations, but it is better to do it locally on a speedy solid-state drive than over a network. “Where does every repository live? The answer is ‘anywhere’. It doesn't matter! We treat repositories like a warm cache on disk, but the source of truth is always the write-ahead log,” Martí noted. We will see how well this approach plays out as Origin moves into being a production service. But if we don’t see stories about Origin outages, then Git managers will know to give object storage a serious look. ®

articles.title: D-Propulse Proposes RDE-Powered Air-Launched Cruise Missile That Could Fly on Tejas Mk1A With BrahMos-A-Class Range
articles.text:
D-Propulse founder and CEO Saurav Jha, speaking on the 50th episode of the Ctrl Alt Defence podcast, outlined an ambitious longer-term application for the company’s Rotating Detonation Engine technology: an air-launched cruise missile capable of exceeding Mach 3 while remaining compact enough to be carried by lighter fighters like the Tejas Mk1A, packing a 200 kg warhead and delivering range comparable to the air-launched BrahMos-A, a weapon currently restricted almost entirely to India’s heavier Su-30MKI fleet.
The Platform Compatibility Problem This Would Solve
To understand why this proposal matters, it helps to understand what BrahMos-A actually is and why it hasn’t reached most of the Indian Air Force’s fighter fleet. The air-launched BrahMos, inducted into IAF service in 2019, carries the same core supersonic performance as its ship- and land-launched siblings, cruising at Mach 3 with a conventional semi-armour-piercing warhead in the 200-300 kg class. But at roughly 2.5 to 2.9 tonnes for the base airframe, it’s simply too heavy and bulky for most Indian fighters to carry, which is why BrahMos-A integration has remained largely confined to the Su-30MKI, the one platform in the IAF inventory with the structural strength and payload capacity to handle it.
DRDO has already been working to solve this exact problem through BrahMos-NG, a compact variant cutting weight to around 1.3 tonnes specifically to fit smaller platforms like Tejas, Rafale, and MiG-29, while targeting broadly similar range in the 290-350 km class at speeds up to Mach 3.5. Jha’s RDE-based proposal pursues a strikingly similar end goal, matching BrahMos-A-class range on a lighter fighter, but through an entirely different propulsion architecture rather than conventional airframe miniaturisation.
Why RDE Propulsion Enables This Kind of Compression
The physics underpinning Jha’s proposal comes down to the same fundamental advantage driving all of D-Propulse’s work: Pressure-Gain Combustion. Because a Rotating Detonation Engine’s continuous supersonic detonation wave increases total pressure through combustion rather than losing it, as happens in conventional deflagration-based engines, the same quantity of fuel yields meaningfully more usable thrust and range. That efficiency gain is precisely what allows Jha to argue a missile built around a compact 5 kN RDE could match BrahMos-A’s range envelope while occupying a substantially smaller airframe, small enough that a lighter single-engine fighter like Tejas Mk1A could plausibly carry it without needing BrahMos-NG’s more extensive weight-reduction redesign.
This isn’t a purely theoretical claim from D-Propulse. The company’s 5 kN air-breathing RDE combustor, integrated with an aerospike nozzle for efficiency across a wide altitude envelope, has already been hot-fired and validated at Technology Readiness Level 5 at a DRDO facility in Hyderabad, giving the propulsion side of this concept a genuine, tested foundation rather than resting on paper calculations alone.
Fitting Into D-Propulse’s Broader Strategic Vision
This air-launched missile concept builds directly on the “mixed-tier” strike doctrine Jha has previously articulated. His broader argument holds that premium weapons like BrahMos, priced between roughly $4.85 million and $5.5 million per unit, are too expensive to expend in the volume needed for saturation strikes against layered enemy air defences. A cheaper, RDE-powered alternative capable of sustained Mach 3-to-5 speeds could instead be produced and deployed in much larger numbers, reserving BrahMos-class munitions specifically for the highest-value targets while a swarm of more affordable RDE missiles handles the work of overwhelming enemy radar and interceptor capacity through sheer volume.
Applying that logic to an air-launched, Tejas-compatible weapon adds a further dimension: it would let the IAF’s large and growing Tejas Mk1A fleet, which currently lacks any organic supersonic standoff strike capability comparable to what the Su-30MKI brings with BrahMos-A, field a genuinely potent long-range strike option without needing the heavier airframe or higher unit cost that BrahMos-NG or the original BrahMos-A require.
From Missile-Scale Engine to Fighter-Relevant Weapon
It’s worth situating this proposal within D-Propulse’s broader, staged roadmap rather than treating it as an imminent, fully engineered product. The company has publicly stated it’s targeting Technology Readiness Level 7, demonstrated through a powered sustainer flight, by December 2027, with fully guided RDE-powered munitions offered for Indian military user trials only by December 2029. An unguided cruise-missile-shaped test vehicle is separately planned for 2027 specifically to validate the RDE engine’s performance in free flight. A dedicated, guided, Tejas-compatible air-launched cruise missile with a 200 kg warhead and BrahMos-A-class range would represent a considerably more mature product than either of those nearer-term milestones, built once the underlying engine technology has been proven across multiple progressively more demanding test phases.
Why This Matters Beyond Just One Missile Programme
Even setting aside the specific Tejas-compatible concept, the broader significance here is what it says about India’s private defence-industrial ecosystem. D-Propulse isn’t alone in pursuing RDE technology for missile applications, other startups like Prime Tooling have separately signalled interest in the same propulsion class for loitering munitions and swarm drone applications, suggesting a maturing private innovation track that’s beginning to move faster on advanced propulsion concepts than some traditional public-sector timelines have historically managed. If even a portion of D-Propulse’s roadmap holds, RDE technology could plausibly extend beyond simply matching existing missile capability to enabling entirely new categories of standoff weapons that current airframe-and-engine combinations can’t achieve, sustained Mach 5-plus speeds in compact packages being the more distant but genuinely transformative long-term promise Jha and others in this space have pointed toward.
The Bottom Line
A Tejas Mk1A-compatible, RDE-powered cruise missile matching BrahMos-A’s range in a meaningfully smaller, lighter package would fill a real capability gap in the IAF’s current fighter fleet, giving India’s most numerous indigenous fighter type genuine long-range supersonic strike capability it currently lacks. The proposal rests on real, tested propulsion hardware rather than pure speculation, but it remains several development stages and multiple years away from an actual guided weapon, sitting behind the unguided 2027 engine-validation flight and the broader TRL-7-by-2027, user-trials-by-2029 roadmap D-Propulse has already committed to publicly.

articles.title: IMRH: India’s Medium-Lift Helicopter Cannot Afford to Wait
articles.text:
The Indian Multi-Role Helicopter (IMRH) is one of the most consequential aerospace programmes India has launched in the past decade — and also one of the most stalled. Designed as a 12–13 tonne twin-engine medium-lift platform to replace the ageing Mi-17 fleet across the Army, Air Force, and Navy, the IMRH sits at the centre of India’s rotary-wing future. Yet despite years of design work, the programme remains blocked at the pre-development stage, awaiting the formal approval of a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) that will determine how HAL, government agencies, and private industry share funding, risks, and responsibilities.
Where the programme stands
As of mid-2026, the joint IMRH and Deck-Based Multi-Role Helicopter (DBMRH) case is at the Pre-Acceptance of Necessity (Pre-AoN) stage, with the Indian Air Force acting as the lead service and HAL as the principal developer. Admiral Dinesh K Tripathi, Chief of the Naval Staff, confirmed in January 2026 that the Navy is seeking the DBMRH in three distinct variants covering surface, sub-surface, and aerial mission profiles. The design has been frozen, HAL is optimistic about Cabinet Committee on Security clearance, and prototypes are expected by 2028, with flight trials beginning in 2029 and certification targeted by 2031.
But every one of those dates depends on something that has not happened yet: the SPV approval. Without it, the programme cannot move from design to hardware.
Why it matters now
The Indian Army alone is projected to require roughly 400 helicopters in the IMRH class, making it one of the largest rotorcraft acquisition opportunities in the country’s history. The Mi-17 fleet, the backbone of India’s medium-lift capability for decades, is ageing. The Air Force, Army, and Navy all need a replacement, and the longer the SPV takes, the wider the capability gap grows.
The IMRH is also not just about the airframe. It is about engine sovereignty. HAL and Safran Helicopter Engines have established a joint venture called SAFHAL to co-develop the “Aravalli” turboshaft engine family — a 3,000+ shaft horsepower powerplant that delivers hot-and-high performance across India’s varied terrain, from Himalayan borders to coastal waters. Unlike earlier arrangements where engines sat outside India’s technology transfer envelope, Aravalli is structured from the outset as a co-developed engine with design centres, test infrastructure, and production in India. If the SPV is delayed further, the engine programme — the most critical subsystem — stalls with it.
A design philosophy built for India
HAL has made deliberate design choices that set the IMRH apart from global competitors. While the world moves toward high-speed tilt-rotor and hybrid platforms, the IMRH prioritises high-altitude performance and heavy lift over raw speed. Its conventional five-bladed articulated rotor system — a departure from the hingeless design used on the Dhruv and LCH — allows it to operate at altitudes approaching 6,000 metres, including Siachen and Ladakh, where hover performance and lift efficiency matter far more than dash speed.
The helicopter also features Manned-Unmanned Teaming (MUM-T) capability, designed as a “mother ship” capable of coordinating with indigenous swarm drones like the Sheshnaag-150, a fully digital glass cockpit with AI-driven decision support, and autonomous flight modes. The DBMRH naval variant adds folding rotors, corrosion-resistant materials, and reinforced landing gear for carrier operations.
“Without these SPVs, both programmes remain stalled at the pre-development stage despite years of design work. Their approval will shape India’s aerospace landscape for the next decade.” — Indian Defence News, July 2026
The competitive pressure
The IMRH also faces emerging industrial competition. Reports of a partnership between Adani Defence & Aerospace and Leonardo S.p.A. to build helicopters locally have drawn attention to the AW101 as a potential licensed alternative. While the IMRH is purpose-built for India’s altitude-driven operational doctrine, a licensed foreign platform could accelerate capability availability — though at the cost of long-term design ownership and the indigenous ecosystem that makes IMRH strategically valuable.
The bottom line is straightforward: India needs to get going on the IMRH programme as soon as possible. Every month of delay at the SPV approval stage pushes prototypes, trials, and certification further into the 2030s, extends Mi-17 service life demands, and widens the gap between design readiness and hardware realisation.

articles.title: BEL’s Microwave Directed Energy Weapon Prototype Ready, User Trials Expected to Begin Soon
articles.text:
Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) has reached another milestone in India’s directed energy weapons (DEW) programme, with the company confirming that its Microwave Directed Energy Weapon (DEW) prototype is now ready and is expected to enter user trials in the near future.
The update indicates that the programme has progressed beyond laboratory development and engineering validation, moving towards operational evaluation by prospective users.
Unlike laser-based directed energy weapons that physically damage targets through concentrated heat, high-power microwave (HPM) weapons disable threats by emitting intense bursts of electromagnetic energy capable of disrupting or damaging electronic circuits, sensors, communications equipment and guidance systems.
Such systems are increasingly viewed as an effective solution against modern battlefield threats, particularly drone swarms, loitering munitions, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), cruise missiles and electronic systems, where conventional kinetic interceptors may prove expensive or inefficient.
BEL has been working closely with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) on several directed energy initiatives, and the readiness of the microwave DEW prototype marks another important step in India’s efforts to develop indigenous non-kinetic weapon systems.
According to the latest programme update, the prototype has completed its development phase and is now preparing for user trials, during which its performance will be evaluated under realistic operational conditions. These trials are expected to validate the system’s effectiveness, reliability, target engagement capability and suitability for military deployment.
Although BEL has not disclosed detailed technical specifications, microwave directed energy weapons are generally designed to engage multiple electronic targets rapidly without relying on conventional ammunition. Their ability to neutralise drones and other electronically dependent systems at the speed of light makes them an attractive option for layered air defence and force protection.
The development complements India’s broader investments in directed energy technologies. DRDO has already demonstrated progress in high-energy laser weapons and is simultaneously advancing microwave-based systems, recognising that both technologies serve different operational roles. Laser systems are primarily intended for precision destruction of targets, while microwave weapons are better suited to disabling or overwhelming electronic systems across a wider area.
If the upcoming user trials prove successful, the microwave DEW could eventually become part of India’s future Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) architecture, providing the armed forces with a reusable, low-cost means of countering increasingly sophisticated aerial threats.

articles.title: DRDO’s Netra Mk1 AEW&CS to Get Multispectral LOROP EO/IR System for 100+ km Imaging
articles.text:
India’s indigenous airborne early warning fleet is set for a major sensor upgrade. DRDO’s Netra Mk1 Airborne Early Warning and Control System (AEW&CS) is reportedly being lined up to receive a Multispectral Long Range Oblique Photography (LOROP) EO/IR system, capable of imaging targets well beyond 100 kilometres in both electro-optical (EO) and infrared (IR) bands.
What Is LOROP and Why It Matters for Netra
LOROP is a long-range, high-magnification imaging technique that lets an aircraft photograph ground targets from extreme standoff distances without entering hostile airspace or contested airspace defended by air defence networks. Instead of flying directly over a target, the sensor uses a large-aperture telephoto optical system, mounted at an oblique angle, to capture high-resolution imagery from far away.
For a platform like Netra — already tasked with airborne early warning, battle management, and situational awareness — adding a multispectral LOROP EO/IR payload converts it into a dual-role asset: part surveillance radar aircraft, part long-range reconnaissance platform. The Indian Air Force has previously outlined a requirement for EO/IR LOROP systems with ranges in excess of 150 km for its broader Intelligence, Surveillance, Target Acquisition and Reconnaissance (ISTAR) roadmap, underscoring how central this sensor class has become to India’s airborne intelligence-gathering plans.
How the EO/IR Multispectral System Works
A multispectral LOROP payload typically combines two imaging channels:
- Electro-Optical (EO) channel — captures high-resolution visible-light imagery, ideal for daytime reconnaissance and precise target identification.
- Infrared (IR) channel — enables imaging in low-light, night, or poor-visibility conditions by detecting heat signatures, making it effective against camouflaged or thermally distinct targets.
Running both channels simultaneously gives operators continuous, all-weather, day-and-night imaging capability from a single stabilized sensor turret — critical for persistent monitoring of borders, troop movements, and strategic installations at ranges beyond 100 km.
Boosting Netra’s Role Beyond Airborne Early Warning
Netra Mk1, built on the Embraer EMB-145 platform, has so far been primarily associated with its Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar, which provides wide-area airborne and maritime target detection. The aircraft recently received Final Operational Clearance (FOC) from DRDO, with reports indicating an upgraded Gallium Nitride (GaN)-based AESA radar has already been fitted to one of the three in-service Mk1 aircraft, extending detection ranges significantly.
Layering a long-range multispectral EO/IR LOROP system onto this radar-centric platform would give the Indian Air Force a single aircraft capable of:
- Detecting and tracking airborne and surface threats via radar
- Visually confirming and imaging targets at long standoff distances
- Operating day or night, regardless of ambient light conditions
- Feeding real-time intelligence to ground stations and fighter aircraft over secure data links
This combination reduces the need to risk manned reconnaissance aircraft or rely solely on satellite passes for time-critical imagery.
Strategic Significance for Border Surveillance
A 100+ km imaging range means the LOROP-equipped Netra could photograph targets deep inside adversary territory while remaining well within Indian airspace or over friendly territory — a significant advantage along sensitive borders. This stand-off imaging capability is particularly valuable for:
- Monitoring military build-ups and troop movements
- Verifying infrastructure changes near contested borders
- Supporting real-time battlefield damage assessment
- Enhancing persistent ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance) coverage without crossing into contested airspace
Such capability aligns with a broader push by DRDO and the IAF toward network-centric, sensor-fused airborne platforms, where AEW&C aircraft double as intelligence hubs rather than pure air-defence radar pickets.
Part of a Larger Netra Modernization Push
The LOROP EO/IR upgrade fits into a wider modernization effort around India’s AEW&C fleet:
- Netra Mk1 — the original three EMB-145-based aircraft, now FOC-certified and receiving GaN AESA radar upgrades
- Netra Mk1A — additional EMB-145-class aircraft planned with more advanced mission systems
- Netra Mk2 — a larger Airbus A321-based platform in development, offering extended radar coverage and endurance
Integrating a long-range EO/IR sensor onto the Mk1 fleet suggests DRDO is looking to maximize the operational value of existing airframes even as the larger Mk2 program matures. It also mirrors global trends, where AWACS-class aircraft increasingly carry auxiliary imaging payloads to support multi-domain awareness rather than radar detection alone.
What This Means for India’s Airborne ISR Capability
If integrated successfully, the multispectral LOROP EO/IR system would make Netra Mk1 one of the few AEW&C-class platforms in the region combining wide-area radar surveillance with long-range photographic reconnaissance in a single airframe. For India, this translates into:
- Reduced dependency on foreign-sourced reconnaissance imagery
- Faster turnaround on time-sensitive intelligence
- A more versatile platform for both peacetime monitoring and contingency operations
As development details firm up, further clarity is expected on the sensor’s exact manufacturer, integration timeline, and whether the upgrade will extend to the upcoming Mk1A and Mk2 variants as well.

articles.title: HAL’s Plan to Build Russia’s SJ-100 in India Draws Mixed Response from Aviation Industry
articles.text:
The proposed agreement between Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation (UAC) to licence-produce the Sukhoi Superjet 100 (SJ-100) regional passenger aircraft in India has sparked a mixed response among commercial aviation experts, airline executives and industry analysts. While supporters believe the programme could strengthen India’s regional aviation ecosystem under the government’s UDAN initiative, critics question its commercial viability, citing the aircraft’s operational history, sanctions-related risks and HAL’s already stretched manufacturing commitments.
Industry observers note that the SJ-100 has struggled to gain widespread acceptance outside Russia over the past decade. Earlier variants of the aircraft faced criticism over maintenance requirements, fleet availability and the timely supply of spare parts. These issues resulted in several international operators reducing or discontinuing their use of the aircraft, creating concerns about its long-term attractiveness in the commercial aviation market.
One of the strongest reservations expressed by airline industry stakeholders relates to commercial adoption. Analysts argue that India’s major private carriers, which typically prioritise fleet commonality, global maintenance support and proven aircraft reliability, are unlikely to voluntarily introduce the SJ-100 into their fleets unless substantial operational and financial incentives are offered.
Another major concern revolves around the impact of international sanctions on Russia. Aviation specialists point out that commercial aircraft operate within a highly interconnected global ecosystem involving internationally certified suppliers, maintenance providers and component manufacturers. Although Russia has been working to increase the indigenous content of the SJ-100, industry experts believe sanctions could continue to complicate the availability of certain components, aftermarket support and international certification pathways.
Some analysts also warn that companies participating in supply chains associated with sanctioned Russian aerospace programmes could face additional compliance and commercial challenges when dealing with Western aerospace manufacturers and financial institutions.
Within India’s defence and aerospace community, another frequently raised issue concerns HAL’s industrial capacity. The company is already managing several major military programmes, including the Tejas Mk1A, Tejas Mk2, Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), Hindustan Turbo Trainer (HTT-40), Light Utility Helicopter (LUH) and production support for multiple helicopter and engine programmes.
Critics argue that adding a complex regional airliner manufacturing programme could place further pressure on HAL’s engineering resources, production facilities and supply chain, particularly when several indigenous defence projects continue to face demanding delivery schedules.
Supporters of the initiative, however, present a different perspective. Rather than viewing the SJ-100 primarily as a competitor to aircraft operated by India’s major airlines, they believe it could serve a niche role in expanding regional air connectivity.
Under the government’s UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) scheme, India is seeking to improve air links to smaller cities and underserved airports. Proponents suggest that a domestically assembled regional jet could support these objectives, particularly if operated through state-backed airlines, public sector operators or specialised leasing arrangements.
They also argue that local production could help develop India’s civil aerospace manufacturing capabilities, diversify HAL’s product portfolio and strengthen domestic expertise in commercial aircraft assembly and support.
Even so, industry experts emphasise that long-term success will ultimately depend on whether the aircraft can demonstrate competitive operating costs, reliable after-sales support and sustained parts availability. Commercial airlines typically base fleet decisions on lifecycle economics rather than geopolitical considerations, making operational reliability and maintenance infrastructure decisive factors.

articles.title: Can Astra Mk-3-Armed Loyal Wingmen Counter a 500-Strong J-20 Fleet? Why India Needs a Much Broader Air Combat Architecture
articles.text:
The prospect of confronting a force of approximately 500 Chengdu J-20 fifth-generation stealth fighters operating along the Himalayan frontier has prompted discussions about whether loyal wingmen armed with India’s upcoming Astra Mk-3 (Gandiva) beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile could provide an effective counter. While the concept of employing large numbers of affordable, attritable unmanned combat aircraft is gaining traction worldwide, defence analysts argue that relying on loyal wingmen alone would be insufficient against a massed fifth-generation force.
The Astra Mk-3, powered by a Solid Fuel Ducted Ramjet (SFDR), is expected to provide a significantly larger no-escape zone and sustained energy at long ranges than conventional solid-rocket missiles. However, missile performance is only one part of the air combat equation. The more decisive factor is the ability to detect, identify, track and continuously update targeting information against low-observable aircraft operating in a heavily contested electromagnetic environment.
The Sensor Challenge
The J-20’s primary advantage lies not only in its stealth characteristics but also in its integration into a broader network of airborne early warning aircraft, electronic intelligence platforms, ground-based sensors and secure data links. In modern air combat, success is increasingly determined by the side that achieves “first detection, first targeting and first engagement.”
A loyal wingman equipped with only its onboard fire-control radar would likely detect a low-observable aircraft at substantially shorter ranges than the missile’s maximum engagement envelope. Without external targeting support, the Astra Mk-3’s long-range capability cannot be fully exploited, because beyond-visual-range missiles require accurate and continuously updated target information throughout much of their flight.
Mountainous terrain further complicates the engagement. The Himalayas create extensive radar shadow zones, terrain masking opportunities and variable line-of-sight conditions that can allow stealth aircraft to approach while reducing the effectiveness of conventional radar systems.
Missile Performance Alone Cannot Offset Network Disadvantages
The Astra Mk-3 is expected to be one of India’s most capable air-to-air missiles, with its ramjet propulsion allowing sustained speed and energy throughout much of its flight. Against conventional fighters, this provides a larger engagement envelope and improved end-game manoeuvrability.
However, missile kinematics cannot compensate for limitations in target acquisition. If a loyal wingman cannot generate or receive a high-quality target track, its missile cannot fully exploit its theoretical range. Stealth aircraft employing electronic warfare, terrain masking and coordinated tactics could further complicate missile engagements.
Payload limitations also matter. Loyal wingmen are generally designed as relatively compact, lower-cost platforms carrying only a limited number of weapons. Even if deployed in large numbers, they would struggle to generate sufficient missile volume to independently counter hundreds of advanced fighters.
A Multi-Layered Counter Is More Realistic
Rather than relying on any single platform, analysts generally argue that countering a large fifth-generation fleet requires an integrated system of systems.
A comprehensive approach could include:
- Multi-band radar architecture, combining VHF, UHF, L-band and X-band sensors to improve detection of low-observable aircraft.
- Distributed sensor networks, including airborne early warning aircraft, high-altitude unmanned systems, aerostats, passive sensors and space-based surveillance.
- Network-centric command and control, allowing targeting data to be shared seamlessly between fighters, loyal wingmen, ground-based air defences and naval assets.
- Long-range air-to-air missiles such as Astra Mk-3 to engage targets once reliable tracking has been established.
- Layered ground-based air defence, including systems such as Project Kusha, S-400 and other indigenous surface-to-air missile networks.
- Electronic warfare and cyber capabilities to disrupt hostile communications, navigation and targeting systems.
- Counter-support operations targeting airborne early warning aircraft, aerial refuelling tankers and other enabling assets that extend the effectiveness of a stealth fighter force.
Loyal Wingmen Still Have an Important Role
Despite these limitations, loyal wingmen remain an important capability multiplier. They can extend sensor coverage, carry additional missiles, conduct electronic warfare, perform decoy missions and accept higher operational risk than manned fighters. Operating alongside aircraft such as the AMCA, Tejas Mk2 or upgraded Su-30MKI, they could increase the number of available sensors and shooters within a networked force.
Rather than replacing manned fighters, loyal wingmen are likely to function as force multipliers within a larger combat ecosystem.
The Future Air Battle
Any future confrontation involving large numbers of fifth-generation aircraft would be determined less by individual fighter performance than by the effectiveness of each side’s integrated combat network. Stealth, sensor fusion, electronic warfare, resilient communications and distributed targeting are increasingly as important as speed, manoeuvrability or missile range.

articles.title: An ultra-rare piece of Microsoft history could be hiding on your shelf
articles.text: In a future edition of The Antiques Roadshow, the hosts might get all excited about a mint Microsoft Entertainment Pack for Windows… with a sticker on the box instead of a printed Tetris promotion. Veteran Microsoft engineer Raymond Chen explained the reasoning behind using the sticker instead of simply printing what was in the box. Microsoft hadn't locked down the rights for Tetris before the first print run of the packaging, so went with what it had. The Microsoft Entertainment Pack for Windows debuted in 1990, the same year that Windows 3.0 was released and ushered in an era of Microsoft desktop dominance. Three more iterations of the entertainment pack followed, which included FreeCell, before Microsoft pulled the plug in 1992 (although a Best Of version arrived in 1994, and there was another version for Windows CE later in the 1990s). We'll draw a discreet veil over the ad-festooned version currently in the Microsoft Store. The floppy disks in the box included several card games, Minesweeper, and a Windows version of the fiendishly addictive and massively popular game of the era, Tetris. But it might not have gone that way. Chen explained in a post on his Old New Thing blog, "At the time the first run of boxes were being printed, the negotiations to license Tetris hadn't yet concluded. There was a chance that the negotiations would fall through, and the Entertainment Pack would have to be released without Tetris." So, rather than risk throwing away a production run, Microsoft went ahead with the Tetris-less branding, and added a sticker when the deal was done. Later print runs made the sticker part of the box art, hence the rarity of the original. Microsoft has a bit of a history of inadvertently creating collectibles. Chen recalled an incident with Windows 95, when an anti-piracy hologram on the case depicted a child pointing at a computer monitor and the Windows 95 logo. The child was shirtless, which caused offense in some quarters. Microsoft's solution? A new hologram with the baby in a shirt and overalls. However, some original versions still exist. Chen said, "So if you still have your copy of Windows 95, go look at the hologram. If the baby in your hologram isn't wearing a shirt, you have a genuine collector's item." We can just imagine the excitement at the recording now, as someone produces not only a stickered version of the Microsoft Entertainment Pack for Windows, but also the topless baby version of Windows 95… ®

articles.title: India 300-5 after Padikkal's 2nd ton of series
Volcanoes that made history
articles.text:
The first telegram arrived in Singapore on a Monday, sent from the city of Batavia in the Dutch East Indies (now Jakarta, Indonesia). “Terrific detonations from Krakatau (volcanic island),” it reported. Soon afterward: “Stones falling. Village near Anjer washed away.” The wires continued clattering out news of bridges destroyed, boats smashed, lighthouses “disappeared.” By noon on Tuesday, the scope of the natural disaster was clear: “Where once Mount Krakatau stood the sea now plays.”

Within days, the source of the destruction was known worldwide. On the morning of August 27, 1883, a volcanic eruption had obliterated two islands in the strait between Java and Sumatra, and most of a third. More than 36,000 people perished, the majority in devastating tsunamis that raced outward from the colossal explosion.

Thanks to Victorian-era telecommunications, it was the first time in history that people around the globe could begin to document, in near real time, the immediate and long-term effects of a catastrophic volcanic eruption. What they learned over the next few years laid the foundations for the modern science of volcanology. And it was an especially eye-opening lesson in how the biggest eruptions can influence climate, agriculture, and even the course of human history.
